title: Building Context-Aware Reasoning Applications with LangChain and LangSmith: Harrison Chase

primary.label: Agent Architecture & Harnesses
primary.rationale: The talk's intellectual core is a taxonomy of cognitive architectures for LLM reasoning (plain code, single LLM call, chains, routers, agent while-loops, autonomous agents) and the orchestration challenge of choosing among them. Chase explicitly covers agent loops, planning patterns (plan-execute-validate), and the control plane around models, which are the defining inclusion criteria for this category.

secondary.label: AI Platforms & Developer Tooling
secondary.rationale: LangChain (an SDK/framework) and LangSmith (a developer platform with playground, tracing, and evaluation tooling) are presented as the substrate other engineers use to build LLM applications. The talk's second half is structured around how these platforms address five engineering challenges.

secondary.label: Context Engineering & Memory
secondary.rationale: A major theme is the four types of context provision to LLMs (instruction prompting, few-shot examples, RAG, fine-tuning) and what enters the model context. The prompt engineering section discusses how fully formatted prompts combine system instructions, few-shot examples, retrieved context, chat history, and prior agent steps.

secondary.label: Prompting & LLM Programming
secondary.rationale: Instruction prompting, few-shot examples, and structured output patterns are discussed as distinct context types. The prompt engineering challenge covers inspecting and editing fully formatted prompts combining multiple components.

domains.label: Developer Platforms
domains.rationale: LangChain and LangSmith are developer tools and platforms used by software builders to construct, debug, and evaluate LLM applications. The talk is addressed to AI engineers at a developer conference.

domains.label: General Purpose
domains.rationale: The cognitive architecture taxonomy and engineering challenges discussed are cross-domain, applicable to any LLM application regardless of vertical. No specific application domain is emphasized.

summary: Harrison Chase, CEO and co-founder of LangChain, delivered this keynote at the AI Engineer Summit 2023 (published November 1, 2023). He argues that LLMs alone are insufficient for building useful applications—they lack knowledge of current events, cannot run code, and don't remember interactions—and must be embedded in larger systems that provide context and reasoning. Chase identifies four types of context provision: instruction prompting (zero-shot, analogous to an employee handbook), few-shot examples (showing rather than telling, good for tone and structured output), retrieval-augmented generation (RAG, an open-book test), and fine-tuning (updating weights, scaling to ~10,000 examples). He then presents a six-level progression of cognitive architectures for reasoning: plain code, single LLM call, chains, routers, agent while-loops, and autonomous agents. The second half details five engineering challenges: orchestration (chains offer control over step sequencing; agents handle edge cases dynamically—neither universally superior), data engineering (context is often data requiring loading, transformation, and transport), prompt engineering (inspecting fully formatted prompts combining system instructions, few-shot, retrieved context, chat history, and prior agent steps), evaluation (hindered by zero-shot MVPs shipping without datasets and lack of metrics for unstructured outputs, addressed via LLM-assisted evaluation and direct/indirect user feedback for A/B testing), and collaboration (bridging data engineers for context and non-technical domain experts for prompting). LangChain and LangSmith are presented as the tooling substrate addressing these challenges, with LangSmith providing tracing, a prompt playground, and evaluation capabilities. Chase repeatedly emphasizes the field is in its infancy and current frameworks may become irrelevant within months.
whyItMatters: The software engineering and AI concepts in this talk are deeply interdependent and form a unified framework. The four context types (instruction prompting, few-shot, RAG, fine-tuning) define what information enters an LLM, while the six-level cognitive architecture taxonomy defines how the LLM reasons over that information. The five engineering challenges—orchestration, data engineering, prompt engineering, evaluation, and collaboration—are the practical disciplines required to turn these theoretical building blocks into production systems. Orchestration decides which cognitive architecture to use; data engineering ensures the right context reaches the model; prompt engineering inspects how that context is composed and formatted; evaluation measures whether the system works and enables iteration; and collaboration determines who builds each part. Together they bridge the gap between raw LLM capability and the engineering complexity behind seemingly magical product experiences. LangChain and LangSmith are positioned as the tooling substrate that operationalizes this entire framework.
temporalContext: Recorded at the AI Engineer Summit 2023 and published November 1, 2023. At this time, LangChain was less than a year old as a company (founded early 2023), LangSmith was in closed beta (announced July 2023, reached GA February 2024), and the LLM application landscape was characterized by rapid early-stage experimentation with autonomous agents like AutoGPT being recent phenomena. Chase's caveat that 'this could be irrelevant in three months' reflects the pace of change in late 2023. Research verification was conducted as of August 2026, by which point LangChain had achieved unicorn status ($1.25B valuation), 35% Fortune 500 adoption, and 1B+ open-source downloads, with LangSmith evolved into a full agent engineering platform. The talk's taxonomy of cognitive architectures and engineering challenges has proven durable, as Chase continued discussing agent harnesses and evaluation in 2026.
takeaways: LLMs alone are insufficient; they must be part of larger systems that provide context and reasoning capabilities
Four types of context: instruction prompting, few-shot examples, RAG, and fine-tuning, each suited to different use cases
Reasoning architectures form a spectrum from deterministic code to fully autonomous agents, each with distinct trade-offs
Chains offer control over step sequencing; agents dynamically react to unexpected inputs and edge cases—neither is universally superior
Building production LLM applications involves five major challenges: orchestration, data engineering, prompt engineering, evaluation, and collaboration
Evaluation is hindered by lack of data (zero-shot capability means MVPs ship without datasets) and lack of good metrics for unstructured outputs
LLM-assisted evaluation and tracking direct/indirect user feedback are promising approaches to closing the evaluation gap
Effective collaboration may require both data engineers (for context) and non-technical domain experts (for prompting), making the AI engineer role still ill-defined
The field is extremely early; current frameworks may become irrelevant within months
Behind seemingly magical LLM product experiences lies extraordinary engineering effort

concepts.name: Context-aware reasoning
concepts.explanation: Building LLM applications that provide appropriate context (what the model knows) and reasoning (how the model processes that knowledge). LangChain is officially described as a framework for building context-aware reasoning applications.
concepts.importance: Overarching paradigm that structures the entire talk; defines the two pillars (context and reasoning) around which all other concepts are organized.

concepts.name: Instruction prompting (zero-shot)
concepts.explanation: Telling the model how to behave via system instructions, analogous to giving a new employee a handbook. The simplest form of context provision.
concepts.importance: Baseline context type against which all others are compared; foundational for understanding the context spectrum.

concepts.name: Few-shot prompting
concepts.explanation: Showing the model examples of desired behavior rather than just telling it. Useful for establishing tone and producing structured output. Typically uses a small number of examples (~3).
concepts.importance: Key context type that bridges instruction and fine-tuning; demonstrates the show-don't-tell approach to context provision.

concepts.name: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG)
concepts.explanation: Providing grounding context by retrieving relevant information at query time, analogous to an open-book test. Grounds LLM responses in external knowledge.
concepts.importance: One of the most widely adopted patterns for production LLM applications; addresses the LLM's lack of current/proprietary knowledge.

concepts.name: Fine-tuning
concepts.explanation: Updating model weights using a large number of examples (~10,000 vs ~3 for few-shot). Suits the same use cases as few-shot (tone, structured data parsing) but at much larger scale.
concepts.importance: Represents the most intensive context provision method; Chase notes best practices are still being figured out.

concepts.name: Cognitive architecture taxonomy
concepts.explanation: A six-level progression of reasoning architectures: plain code (fully deterministic), single LLM call, chains (known sequential steps), routers (model selects steps without loops), agent while-loops (model decides steps and termination), and autonomous agents (dynamic tool creation, implicit plan-execute-validate).
concepts.importance: Intellectual core of the talk; provides the vocabulary and mental model for reasoning about LLM application design choices.

concepts.name: Autonomous agents
concepts.explanation: The highest level of cognitive architecture: agents that dynamically create tools, implicitly follow a plan-execute-validate pattern with minimal scaffolding, à la AutoGPT.
concepts.importance: Represents the frontier of LLM application autonomy; illustrates the trade-off between flexibility and control at the extreme.

concepts.name: LLM-assisted evaluation
concepts.explanation: Using LLMs to evaluate the outputs of other LLMs, a promising approach to closing the evaluation gap when traditional quantitative metrics don't perform well for unstructured outputs.
concepts.importance: Practical strategy for addressing the evaluation bottleneck; increasingly central to production LLM workflows.

concepts.name: Plan-execute-validate pattern
concepts.explanation: An implicit pattern in autonomous agents where the system plans, executes, and validates without explicit scaffolding for each phase.
concepts.importance: Describes the operational logic of autonomous agents; relevant for understanding emergent agent behavior.

concepts.name: Zero-shot MVP capability
concepts.explanation: LLMs' zero-shot capability allows teams to reach a working minimum viable product without building any datasets, which is advantageous for speed but creates evaluation challenges downstream.
concepts.importance: Explains why evaluation is uniquely hard for LLM applications compared to traditional software; a distinguishing characteristic of the domain.

concepts.name: LLM chains
concepts.explanation: Cognitive architecture where known sequential steps are executed, potentially interleaving LLM and API calls. Provides deterministic control over step sequencing.
concepts.importance: The most commonly used production architecture for LLM applications at the time of the talk; serves as the baseline for comparison with agent architectures.

concepts.name: Router architecture
concepts.explanation: A cognitive architecture where the LLM determines which steps, prompts, models, or tools to use at runtime, without looping back. More flexible than chains but bounded unlike agents.
concepts.importance: Represents a key intermediate design point in the architecture taxonomy; useful when some dynamic selection is needed but full agent loops are excessive.

concepts.name: Orchestration (cognitive architecture selection)
concepts.explanation: Choosing the right cognitive architecture for an LLM application—chains for deterministic control over step sequencing, agents for dynamic handling of unexpected inputs and edge cases. Neither is universally superior; the choice depends on the use case.
concepts.importance: Central organizing principle of the talk; determines the structure and behavior of the entire LLM application.

concepts.name: Chain pattern (predetermined sequential steps)
concepts.explanation: A cognitive architecture where steps are known in advance and executed sequentially, potentially interleaving LLM and API calls. Offers control over the sequence of operations.
concepts.importance: One of the two primary architectural patterns discussed; foundational for understanding structured LLM application design.

concepts.name: Agent loop pattern (while-loop with dynamic termination)
concepts.explanation: A cognitive architecture where the LLM decides what steps to take and when to stop, cycling through a loop. Enables dynamic reaction to unexpected inputs and edge cases.
concepts.importance: Represents a major paradigm shift from deterministic to dynamic LLM application design; core to the agent architecture taxonomy.

concepts.name: Router pattern (model selects steps without loops)
concepts.explanation: A cognitive architecture where the LLM determines which steps, prompts, models, or tools to use but without looping back, giving more flexibility than chains while remaining bounded.
concepts.importance: Bridges the gap between fully deterministic chains and open-ended agent loops; a key intermediate architecture in the taxonomy.

concepts.name: Data engineering for LLM context
concepts.explanation: Loading, transforming, and transporting data that becomes LLM context. Since context is often data, engineering pipelines must ensure documents are extracted correctly and formatted clearly by the time they reach the model.
concepts.importance: Context quality directly determines LLM output quality; data engineering is a prerequisite for effective RAG and few-shot systems.

concepts.name: Prompt engineering (fully formatted prompt inspection)
concepts.explanation: Understanding and debugging the fully formatted prompt that combines system instructions, few-shot examples, retrieved context, chat history, and prior agent steps. LangSmith enables inspecting any LLM call at any point, editing prompts, and swapping model providers.
concepts.importance: As systems scale, the composed prompt becomes opaque; prompt engineering is a critical debugging and iteration skill.

concepts.name: LLM application evaluation
concepts.explanation: Evaluation is hard due to lack of data (zero-shot capability lets teams ship MVPs without datasets) and lack of good metrics for unstructured outputs. Strategies include building datasets from labeling, production traffic, or LLM auto-generation, and using LLM-assisted evaluation.
concepts.importance: Evaluation is the bottleneck for moving from prototype to production; without it, teams cannot confidently iterate or deploy.

concepts.name: A/B testing for LLM applications
concepts.explanation: Tracking direct user feedback (thumbs up/down) and indirect feedback (link clicks, confused responses) to enable A/B testing of LLM application variants.
concepts.importance: Provides the empirical signal needed to compare architectural and prompt variants in production.

concepts.name: Observability and tracing for LLM systems
concepts.explanation: Inspecting LLM calls at any point in an application to understand tool sequences, data flow, and intermediate outputs. LangSmith provides tracing, a playground for editing prompts, and the ability to swap model providers.
concepts.importance: As LLM applications grow complex, visibility into intermediate steps is essential for debugging and optimization.

concepts.name: Dataset construction for LLM evaluation
concepts.explanation: Building evaluation datasets from manual labeling, production traffic, or LLM auto-generation to close the data gap created by zero-shot MVPs that ship without any datasets.
concepts.importance: Without evaluation datasets, teams cannot measure quality improvements or detect regressions in LLM applications.

concepts.name: Cross-functional collaboration in AI engineering
concepts.explanation: Context awareness often needs data engineers, while reasoning via prompting may be best done by non-technical domain experts or product managers. The ideal AI engineer skill set remains unclear.
concepts.importance: Highlights the organizational challenge of building LLM applications; the AI engineer role is still being defined.

concepts.name: Production system design (LLMs as components)
concepts.explanation: LLMs must be embedded as components in larger systems that provide context and reasoning, rather than used in isolation. Behind seemingly magical product experiences lies extraordinary engineering effort.
concepts.importance: Foundational framing of the entire talk; shifts focus from model capability to system architecture.

sections.title: Introduction: LLMs as One Part of a Larger System
sections.summary: Chase opens by noting ChatGPT is just the beginning. LLMs alone lack current events, code execution, and memory of interactions. Truly personalized AI assistants require LLMs as components in larger systems. LangChain aims to help teams close the gap between magical experiences and the engineering required.

sections.title: Types of Context for Language Models
sections.summary: Chase describes four context types: instruction prompting (like an employee handbook), few-shot examples (showing rather than telling, good for tone and structured output), RAG (open-book test analogy, grounding responses in retrieved context), and fine-tuning (updating weights, scaling few-shot use cases to ~10,000 examples, suited for tone and structured data parsing).

sections.title: Levels of Cognitive Architecture for Reasoning
sections.summary: Chase presents a progression: plain code (fully deterministic), single LLM call (model determines output only), chains (known sequential steps, possibly interleaving LLM and API calls), routers (model selects which steps/prompts/models/tools to use, no loops), agent while-loops (cycles where model decides steps and termination), and autonomous agents (dynamic tool creation, implicit plan-execute-validate, minimal scaffolding, à la AutoGPT).

sections.title: Transition: Still Extremely Early
sections.summary: Chase emphasizes the field is still in its infancy, and the presented frameworks could become irrelevant within months. He transitions toward discussing what it takes to build these systems under the hood.

sections.title: Engineering Challenges: Orchestration and Observability
sections.summary: Chase details the first challenge: choosing the right cognitive architecture. Chains provide control over step sequencing; agents dynamically handle edge cases. Neither is universally superior. LangChain helps teams prototype across architectures, while LangSmith provides visibility into tool sequences and LLM calls as applications grow complex.

sections.title: Engineering Challenges: Data Engineering
sections.summary: Context is often data. Teams need to load, transform, and transport data, then observe what reaches the LLM. LangChain offers open-source modules for data loading and transformation; LangSmith helps debug whether documents were extracted correctly and formatted clearly by the time they arrive at the model.

sections.title: Engineering Challenges: Prompt Engineering
sections.summary: Understanding the fully formatted prompt—combining system instructions, few-shot examples, retrieved context, chat history, and prior agent steps—is critical but becomes difficult as systems scale. LangSmith lets developers inspect any LLM call at any point, open it in a playground, edit prompts, and swap model providers.

sections.title: Engineering Challenges: Evaluation
sections.summary: Evaluation is hard due to lack of data (zero-shot capability lets teams ship MVPs without datasets) and lack of good metrics for unstructured outputs. Chase recommends building datasets from manual labeling, production traffic, or LLM auto-generation; using LLM-assisted evaluation; and tracking direct (thumbs up/down) and indirect (link clicks, confused responses) user feedback for A/B testing.

sections.title: Engineering Challenges: Collaboration and Closing
sections.summary: Collaboration is an open challenge: context awareness needs data engineers, while reasoning via prompting may be best done by non-technical domain experts or PMs. The ideal AI engineer skill set remains unclear. Chase closes by reaffirming the field is still extremely early, will get crazier, and requires significant engineering supported by tools like LangChain and LangSmith.

organization.name: LangChain
organization.summary: LangChain, Inc. is a privately held AI infrastructure company headquartered in San Francisco, California, founded in early 2023 by Harrison Chase and Ankush Gola. The company develops open-source frameworks (LangChain, LangGraph, Deep Agents) and the LangSmith commercial platform for building, debugging, testing, evaluating, and deploying AI agents and LLM applications. The LangChain open-source framework has over 144,000 GitHub stars and 1 billion+ downloads. The company has raised over $160M in total funding, achieving unicorn status at $1.25B valuation in October 2025. LangChain works with 35% of the Fortune 500 and ingests over 1 billion events per day on LangSmith.
organization.status: Active, privately held company. Achieved unicorn status with $1.25B valuation in October 2025 following a $125M funding round backed by Sequoia Capital, Benchmark, and IVP. Headquartered in San Francisco with offices in New York, Boston, and Amsterdam. Employs approximately 265 people. Products include LangSmith (commercial platform), LangChain (open-source framework), LangGraph (agent orchestration framework), and Deep Agents (autonomous agent harness).

technologies.label: LangChain Framework
technologies.summary: LangChain is the open-source framework for building context-aware reasoning applications with LLMs. It provides modules for orchestration (choosing cognitive architectures from chains to agents), data engineering (loading and transforming data into LLM context), and experimentation across architectural patterns. Chase presents it as the primary tooling substrate that helps teams close the gap between magical LLM experiences and the engineering effort required behind the scenes. The framework's official description as 'a framework for building context-aware reasoning applications' matches the talk's framing exactly, as independently verified by the Latent Space interview (September 2023).
technologies.role: Primary product framework discussed throughout the talk; Chase presents LangChain as the tooling substrate addressing all five engineering challenges: orchestration, data engineering, prompt engineering, evaluation, and collaboration

technologies.label: LangSmith Platform
technologies.summary: LangSmith is LangChain's platform for debugging, testing, evaluating, and monitoring LLM applications. It provides tracing for understanding tool sequences and LLM calls, a playground for inspecting and editing fully formatted prompts (combining system instructions, few-shot examples, retrieved context, chat history, and prior agent steps) at any point in an application, and LLM-assisted evaluation capabilities. At the time of the talk (November 2023), LangSmith was in closed beta, having been announced July 18, 2023; it reached general availability on February 15, 2024.
technologies.role: Secondary product demonstrated in the talk; Chase shows LangSmith UI screenshots for tracing and debugging complex systems, and demonstrates the playground for opening any LLM call mid-application, editing prompts directly, and swapping model providers

technologies.label: LLM Cognitive Architecture Taxonomy
technologies.primary: Cognitive Architecture Taxonomy for LLM Reasoning
technologies.summary: Chase presents a six-level progression of cognitive architectures for LLM reasoning: plain code (fully deterministic), single LLM call (model determines output only), chains (known sequential steps), routers (model selects steps without loops), agent while-loops (model decides steps and termination in a loop), and autonomous agents (dynamic tool creation, implicit plan-execute-validate, minimal scaffolding). The taxonomy provides the vocabulary for reasoning about LLM application design choices and the trade-offs between control (chains) and flexibility (agents). Chase explicitly notes that neither chains nor agents are universally superior.
technologies.role: Intellectual core of the talk; Chase presents the six-level progression as the conceptual framework for understanding the orchestration challenge and the trade-offs between control and flexibility in LLM application design

technologies.label: Context Provision Techniques
technologies.summary: Chase identifies four types of context provision for LLMs, forming a spectrum of increasing investment: instruction prompting (zero-shot, analogous to an employee handbook), few-shot examples (showing rather than telling, good for tone and structured output, typically 3 examples), retrieval-augmented generation (RAG, an open-book test grounding responses in retrieved context), and fine-tuning (updating weights with approximately 10,000 examples, suited for tone and structured data parsing at scale). Each suits different use cases and addresses the fundamental limitation that LLMs alone lack current events, code execution, and memory of previous interactions.
technologies.role: One of two main pillars of the talk; Chase identifies four types of context provision to LLMs (instruction prompting, few-shot examples, RAG, fine-tuning) and explains when each is appropriate, defining what information enters the model
